content: Neem oil is a type of vegetable oil that is extracted from the fruits and seeds of the neem tree, scientifically known as Azadirachta indica. This tree is an evergreen species native to the Indian subcontinent, though it has been introduced to various tropical regions worldwide. Among the commercially available products derived from the neem tree, neem oil is considered one of the most significant. Neem oil typically ranges in color from light to dark brown. It has a distinctly bitter taste and a strong odor, often described as a combination of peanut and garlic scents. The oil is primarily composed of triglycerides and contains a significant amount of triterpenoid compounds, which are responsible for its characteristic bitterness. Due to its hydrophobic nature, neem oil cannot mix with water directly and requires the addition of suitable surfactants to emulsify it for practical applications. In terms of its chemical composition, neem oil contains steroids such as campesterol, beta-sitosterol, and stigmasterol. It is also rich in triterpenoids, with azadirachtin being the most prominent and extensively studied compound. The concentration of azadirachtin in neem oil can vary significantly, ranging from 300 parts per million (ppm) to over 2000 ppm, depending on the quality of the neem seeds used during extraction. Neem oil is not utilized for culinary purposes. However, in countries like India and Bangladesh, it is widely used in the production of cosmetics, including soaps, hair care products, body creams, and hand creams. Additionally, it plays a significant role in traditional medicine systems such as Ayurveda, Unani, and folklore medicine, where it is employed to address a broad spectrum of health conditions. Historically, neem oil has been used to treat skin disorders, inflammatory conditions, and fevers. More recently, it has been recognized for its potential in managing rheumatic diseases and as an insect repellent and insecticide. In Ayurvedic medicine, neem oil has been traditionally used to treat conditions such as fever, leprosy, malaria, ophthalmia (eye inflammation), and tuberculosis. Folk medicine practices have also utilized neem oil for its anthelmintic (anti-parasitic), antifeedant (insect deterrent), antiseptic, diuretic, emmenagogue (menstrual flow stimulant), contraceptive, febrifuge (fever-reducing), parasiticide, pediculocide (lice treatment), and insecticidal properties. It has also been employed in the treatment of tetanus, urticaria (hives), eczema, scrofula (lymph node inflammation), and erysipelas (a bacterial skin infection). Traditional methods of administering neem oil and its extracts include oral, vaginal, and topical applications. Neem oil has a long history of use in India and neighboring regions for its therapeutic benefits. Puri (1999) provides a detailed account of the traditional applications, therapeutic indications, and pharmacological studies related to neem oil in his comprehensive work on the subject.
